statement: In 10 volunteers given slowly increasing propofol (64 channels, 2 s multitaper windows), loss of consciousness came with a rise of low-frequency (0.1 to 1 Hz) and alpha (8 to 12 Hz) power, the alpha increase concentrated frontally while a spatially coherent occipital alpha mode gave way to a frontal one; low-frequency power was more than 10-fold above baseline while unconscious, and the frontal median frequency fell from 23.1 to 12.0 Hz before loss of consciousness; a clinical review puts the amplitudes of the anesthetized signatures at 5 to 20 times those of the awake EEG. Commercial depth-of-anesthesia indices settle 14 to 155 s after an artificial change of input and 24 ± 7 to 122 ± 23 s after a change between recorded awake, anesthetized and suppressed EEG.

statement: Consumer EEG products are marketed as reading mental states. A review of direct-to-consumer EEG wellness devices categorizes the behavioral and wellness claims their makers publish; a scoping review of 916 studies that used consumer headsets describes a single-forehead-electrode headset whose app reports built-in “meditation” and “attention” metrics, which an independent test found poorly accurate; a test of two headsets in 10 people records the maker’s claim that the single-channel device detects “focused” and “relaxed” states, finds both devices’ attention and meditation outputs highly variable, and the single-channel device below 50% on some concentration-relaxation tasks against above 75% for a 14-channel device; a systematic review of low-cost headsets records a headband claimed to help its wearer reach deep relaxation and a headset that outputs attention and meditation parameters, with drowsiness detection as the surveyed research use; and a comparison of medical and consumer wireless systems names meditation and relaxation training and coping with anxiety or pain as the popular consumer applications. Sleep staging by a consumer headband is covered by claim sleep-scoring-agreement.
note_on_site: The site names the marketed states generically; vendor names appear only in the sources.
sources: Wexler A, Thibault R (2019). Mind-Reading or Misleading? Assessing Direct-to-Consumer Electroencephalography (EEG) Devices Marketed for Wellness and Their Ethical and Regulatory Implications. Journal of Cognitive Enhancement 3(1):131–137. doi:10.1007/s41465-018-0091-2

statement: Measured accuracies of passive EEG state classifiers: two workload levels from 2 s windows, 76.1% on average within person (58.7 to 95.4%; chance 53.1% by a binomial test over 1,080 windows), 96% when 45 windows are pooled, and 3 to 4 points lower in a different affective context (24 people); in a 90 min memory task a band-power chain scored 60% and drifted over the session while a probe-evoked-potential chain scored 91% (20 people); workload networks scored 87.1% on the task they were trained on and 44.8% across tasks; with no data from the test person, two workload levels were classified at 79.1% from 5 s windows to 86.8% from 30 s in 8 people, and the classic 1998 comparison gave 83% for a group classifier against 94% for individually trained ones; with small samples, classifiers applied to pure noise reach two-class “accuracies” of 70% or more, so nominal chance understates what counts as above chance.
sources: Muhl C, Jeunet C, Lotte F (2014). EEG-based workload estimation across affective contexts. Frontiers in Neuroscience 8:114. doi:10.3389/fnins.2014.00114

note_for_auditor: Mühl 2014 (open): 76.1% (58.7–95.4), chance 53.1% over 1,080 trials, 96% over 45 trials, 3–4 points cross-context, n = 24. Roy 2016 abstract: 60% vs 91%, 20 participants, 90 min. Baldwin 2012 abstract: 87.1% and 44.8%. Hefron 2018 (open, Sensors): Table 2 0.791 (5 s) to 0.868 (30 s), 8 participants, and its quotation of Gevins 1998 (83% vs 94%). Combrisson 2015 abstract: 70% on noise.

statement: Resting band power varies widely between people: in 6,029 adults recorded with a four-channel headband (eyes closed), the standard deviation of log10 band power across people of the same age was about 0.21 to 0.36 for delta, theta, alpha and beta at AF7, AF8, TP9 and TP10, a factor of 1.6 to 2.3 in power per standard deviation and three to four times the spread of the age means; log-transformed absolute power is approximately normal across healthy people, and between-person differences in eyes-closed power are largely heritable traits (760 twins and siblings). The model takes 0.65 natural-log units (0.28 log10) as the spread of each region’s resting log power between people.
note_on_site: The standard deviations are read from the paper’s Figure 3, not printed; they include measurement noise and session-to-session change, so they bound the trait spread from above.
sources: Hashemi A, Pino LJ, Moffat G, Mathewson KJ, Aimone C, Bennett PJ, Schmidt LA, Sekuler AB (2016). Characterizing Population EEG Dynamics throughout Adulthood. eNeuro 3(6):ENEURO.0275-16.2016. doi:10.1523/ENEURO.0275-16.2016

Gasser 1982 abstract (log transform normalizes). Smit 2005 abstract (heritability, 760). The 0.65 is the site’s choice (0.28 log10 × 2.303).

statement: The same person’s resting band power is stable but not fixed: over 14 days in 90 adults (64 channels, eyes open), the intraclass correlation of log10 absolute power averaged over electrodes was 0.66 for delta, 0.77 for theta, 0.88 for alpha and 0.81 for beta (relative power 0.75, 0.80, 0.86 and 0.79), with split-half consistency within a session of 0.93 to 0.98; broad-band spectral features correlated 0.92 across 5 min and 0.84 across 12 to 16 weeks in 19 adults; posterior alpha amplitude correlated 0.72 across twelve years in 70 people. The model uses the 14-day intraclass correlations per band: the share 1 − ICC of the between-person variance changes from day to day.
sources: Ziogas A, Ruch S, Skieresz NH, Marca SC, Rothen N, Reber TP (2026). Test-retest reliability analysis of resting-state EEG measures and their association with long-term memory in children and adults. Imaging Neuroscience 4:IMAG.a.1224. doi:10.1162/IMAG.a.1224
